text: Where Jev can and cannot go

TypeSafe's Jev is not a cheaper LLM. It answers typed questions — a probability, a choice among options the caller names, a position on a scale the caller orders — and returns nothing else. That settles the one question this design cannot negotiate: the check leg, whose whole product is a finding quoting the author's clause and the evidence against it, stays an LLM on OpenRouter. Everything Jev takes on below is a leg whose answer was already a choice, or can be made one by moving the string work into code.
What was measured

Every leg was measured on the corpora and adjudications the LLM legs were graded on, three draws each, and every number here re-derives offline from files committed under scripts/verifier-eval — no network, no key. Each leg was measured alone, with the others left as they ship; no run combines two Jev legs. That limit shapes the recommendation below more than any single result does.

**The refuter.** Asked whether a proposed `fact` finding really disagrees with its evidence — the question `REFUTE_SYSTEM` already asks as a choice of three words — Jev lands between the two LLM refuters on the same findings, at a hundredth of their cost and under a second.

**The gate.** Asked before the check leg whether a subject is worth checking, Jev fails when the question is "is anything here wrong" and works when it is "which of these units is wrong, or none" — the units then compete for one probability, and a clean subject puts it on NONE. That presentation saves 58% of the check leg's cost on `fact` and 21% on `claim` without skipping a subject that carried a real defect, and on `claim` it also removes a third of the check leg's false alarms. On `prose` nothing separates. The thresholds are fitted to the same few positives they are scored on, so "none skipped" is an in-sample result with a margin, not a guarantee.

**Classify.** `split`'s first call only sorts the author's own words into current, proposed and argument, so the sorting can be mechanical and the labelling a choice. With Jev's labels in front of the same LLM check, the `claim` verb raises the same number of correct warnings for 39% of the cost — because the classify call, which reads the claim alone and was assumed to be the cheap one, is about half of a `split` verification's spend. One number is unresolved: Jev's arm flagged two more sound claims than the LLM's, across the design's steering-hazard line.

**Literals.** The literal leg already decides every factual part of its finding in code; with code also proposing the candidates, Jev's judgement matches the LLM's at a sixth of the cost and is far more stable. The leg's own problem is unchanged: added to today's check it costs attention the steering-hazard line cannot spare. Behind the claim gate it fits.
**Which Jev.** The measurements name the alias `jev-latest`. The endpoint resolves that alias to a version and says which in every reply, and the benchmark never kept the answer; the design has to.

Every leg was measured on the corpora and adjudications the LLM legs were graded on, three draws each. Each leg was measured alone, with the others left as they ship: no run has measured the configuration this design would ship, where the gate, Jev classify and Jev literals run together. That limit shapes the recommendation below more than any single result does.

text: The design

**One key, and a vendor that routes.** An author turns Jev on with `tetel config verify.typed_model typesafe/jev-1.13.0`. The vendor half `typesafe` is what sends a call to TypeSafe instead of OpenRouter, so the existing model-name syntax needs nothing new, and the credential comes only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment, exactly as OPENROUTER_API_KEY does. There is deliberately no `verify.provider`: the check leg stays on OpenRouter whatever such a key said, so it would name a choice nobody can make. And `verify.model` refuses a `typesafe/` value when it is set, not when a mint fails on it.

**What the key turns on is decided per verb, in source.** On `fact`: a gate before the check. On `claim`: a different gate, Jev classify, and Jev judging literals if literals are on. On `prose`: nothing. Each row is exactly what was measured on that verb, and nothing measured on one verb is carried to another — `fact` shares its classify prompt with `claim` and the literal leg takes no verb at all, so without an explicit table either would silently run a Jev leg nobody measured there. Each leg also ships with the presentation it was measured with, splitter and score included, because the numbers belong to the presentation.

**A gated mint says it was gated.** The gate asks first, before classify. A subject it skips reports a new status, `gated`, rather than `ok` with nothing in it — the whole status vocabulary exists so that an empty result cannot pass for a clean one. A gate that fails never skips anything: the check runs and the response says `gate_incomplete`. The gate's probability is not shown to anyone.

**Nothing changes for anyone who does not set the key.** `verify.typed_model` is unset by default, and `verify.literals` stays off even when it is set. Both defaults wait on the same thing: one joint run of the configuration that would ship — gate, Jev classify, check and Jev literals together — showing the sound claims it flags stay under the design's line, counted per claim. Every figure above that joins two legs was assembled from runs of one leg each.

**The refuter can be Jev, but not over Jev's own judgements.** `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value and asks REFUTE_SYSTEM's three-way question as a choice; its default stays the LLM, since Jev's refuter numbers cover `fact`'s `contradicts` findings alone. The rule that a model may not refute itself — measured at 17% for an LLM — extends to the typed legs, and a refuter call that fails is reported as `refuter_incomplete` instead of passing unrefuted findings off under a printed refuter.

**The version is part of the result.** The thresholds are fitted to one version's probabilities, so the code records which version was measured, prints the one that answered, and says `typed_model_unmeasured` when they differ. A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY is `unauthorized`, naming the variable — never a quiet fall back to the LLM legs under a printed typed model. And the typed legs get a budget sized to calls that take about a second, not the sixty seconds an LLM leg is given.
Rejected alternatives

Jev as the check model, and a `verify.provider` key that would pretend to offer it; one key per typed leg; a gate asked of the whole note; gate criteria rewritten for recall; the capture placed before the author's text; a gate on `prose`; and a Jev probability surfaced to the author as a confidence. Each is rejected on a measurement or on a property of the code, not on taste, and the numbers are above.
Implementation surface and what must hold

The change lives in src/verify.rs and src/config.rs, with docs/verify.md gaining the new key. The declared targets are censused below; `run()` changes too and is named rather than declared, and the `Status` to change is the verifier's, not the ledger's enum of the same name. Four pieces of prose the change falsifies — or that are already false — move with it, including the comment that calls the classify/check cost ratio unmeasured: on `claim` the classify call is about half of a `split` verification.

Eight invariants carry the design, each with the revert its test must turn red: unset means unchanged; skipped means `gated`; a failed gate means checked; `verify.model` cannot be Jev; no model refutes its own judgement; no credential means `unauthorized`; a different version is flagged; and each verb runs only its own row. Their demonstration, green with the fix and red under the revert, is owed when the code exists.

Run this session: the endpoint's response shape and version alias, by a live call; every measurement above, re-derived from committed files by the scorers that produced it. Owed before any default changes: the joint run of the shipping configuration on `claim`, which decides both whether `verify.typed_model` becomes the default and whether `verify.literals` does, and which also settles which side of the steering line Jev classify falls. Owed at code time: the eight invariants' demonstrations. No claim here is a can't-build.
